centralObject.ref: The reciprocal U.S.–China tariff-cut lists released 2026-09-28 by the U.S. Trade Representative and China's commerce ministry: about $30 billion of goods each way (1,619 U.S. items into China; 77 categories of Chinese goods into the U.S.), over 90% moved to most-favored-nation rates, following the 2026-09-24 Trump–Xi meeting
centralObject.name: The 30-for-30 lists

title: Fireworks and Soccer Balls
prompt: The U.S. and China cut tariffs on $30 billion of goods each way. Is this the start of a real thaw, or a small trade that leaves the big tariffs standing?
framing: On Monday, September 28, 2026, the United States and China released matching lists of goods, about $30 billion on each side, that will get lower tariffs. China's list covers 1,619 American items, including farm commodities, timber, medical equipment and coal; soybeans are not on it. The U.S. list covers 77 categories of Chinese goods, such as fireworks, tableware and soccer balls. More than 90% of the products move to standard "most-favored-nation" rates, which are often in the single digits. Chips, electric vehicles and batteries are left out. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the lists cover "nonsensitive goods." The lists follow President Trump's September 24 White House meeting with Xi Jinping, and the two sides extended their trade truce by two months. One estimate has the average U.S. tariff on Chinese goods falling from about 22% to 20.5%.

split.seam: at the centers, the institutional right peels off from the other three stations; at the rim the seam returns to x
split.rationale: The stated object runs along x, but the centers don't. Only B reads the lists as working as designed (+0.45 fluid). A's fluid (−0.15), C's fluid (−0.45) and D's fluid (−0.25) all read a small trade that leaves the wall standing, and the missing soybeans put the right-populist center on the left's side of zero. The coalitions cross over: the institutional left's coalition band goes positive (+0.15) because it has called tariffs a consumer tax for years and can't sneer at a cut, while the populist-right coalition sits near zero (+0.05) between loyalty and soybeans. The rims sort cleanly on x by trust in the holder (Trump): −0.6 / +0.75 / −0.85 / +0.55. A peel at the centers, an axis at the rim; the slider stays on x because the stated object is on x.

zPattern.note: Centers are fluid z; coalition z: A 0.15, B 0.2, C -0.2, D 0.05. D changes sign twice: fluid −0.25, coalition +0.05, rim +0.55. A changes sign fluid → coalition (−0.15 → +0.15) and back at the rim (−0.6).

antiValentRationale: At the rim the goods are gone (no fireworks, no timber, no percentages): the lists become a photo op or a deal for insiders on the left, and proof that China came to Trump on the right.

z.pos: the lists deliver: a real thaw, with lower prices here and open markets for American goods there
z.neg: the lists fail: a token trade that leaves the big tariffs standing and farmers and workers where they were

fluid.zReason: Moving about $30 billion each way to most-favored-nation rates lowers prices on some consumer goods, but the average tariff only falls from about 22% to 20.5%, and chips, EVs and batteries are left out, so the tariff wall is mostly still there.

instrument.holder: the negotiated lists and their annual review

fluid.text: Look, a tariff cut on tableware and soccer balls is still a price cut, and I'll take one wherever I can get it. But the average going from about 22% to 20.5%? That's a rounding error on a tax American households are still paying, and the chips, EVs and batteries are all still walled off.

coalition.zReason: MFN rates on 1,619 American items and 77 Chinese categories are real trade liberalization, and the annual adjustment gives the lists room to grow.

instrument.holder: career trade negotiators and the annual list review

coalition.text: This is a real step toward normal trade, even if it's a small one, and the lists can be adjusted every year. I've heard people on my side wave it off just because Trump's name is on it, and I get the instinct. But I spent years saying tariffs are a tax on consumers, so how do I sneer when some of them come down?

denominated.zReason: The speaker sees Trump as the holder and doesn't trust him, so a point and a half off the average counts as cleanup of damage he did himself, not a thaw.
denominated.text: It's a photo op priced at a point and a half. He built the tariff wall and now he wants credit for putting in a door.

fluid.zReason: The lists move nonsensitive goods to normal rates and open China to American timber, coal, medical equipment and farm commodities, while chips, EVs and batteries stay protected, so the leverage survives.

instrument.holder: Greer and the U.S. Trade Representative's office

fluid.text: This does exactly what it was built to do. Nonsensitive goods get normal rates, American timber, coal and medical equipment get a way into China, and chips, EVs and batteries stay protected. Leaving soybeans off stings, but that's what APEC and the G20 are for.

coalition.zReason: $30 billion each way at MFN rates is trade coming unstuck, but a two-month truce extension and a small drop in the average make it a start, not a settlement.
coalition.text: I think it works, as a start. $30 billion each way is real trade getting unstuck. But I've heard people I usually agree with calling it a breakthrough, and it isn't one: the average only drops to about 20.5%, soybeans aren't on China's list, and the truce is only extended two months. Oversell it now and it looks foolish if the truce lapses.

denominated.zReason: The speaker trusts Trump and his negotiators as the holder, so the swap reads as proof that pressure got China to the table.
denominated.text: This is disciplined deal-making: give on soccer balls, keep the chips. Trump brought Xi to the table and got China to open the door to American goods.

fluid.zReason: Soybeans, the crop hit hardest, aren't on China's list, and cheaper imported fireworks and tableware don't change the tariff picture for factory workers, so the people most exposed stay where they were.

instrument.holder: the two governments and the big exporters

fluid.text: Soybeans aren't on the list. For a lot of farm towns that's the whole story: timber and coal get a break, but the crop that took the worst of it gets nothing. And cheaper fireworks don't do anything about jobs here, one way or the other.

coalition.zReason: Leaving out soybeans and moving the average only a little mean limited delivery, but farm commodities and timber on China's list could still open real doors for some growers.
coalition.text: It doesn't do much for the people I care about: no soybeans, and the average barely moves. But I'm watching folks on my side call it a sellout before anyone even knows how the U.S. side gets implemented. Some farm and timber exporters might actually get an opening, so why not see what happens before scoring it?

denominated.zReason: The speaker sees the holders as Trump and corporate traders and doesn't trust them, so the lists read as a deal for insiders.
denominated.text: Another deal cut at the White House for people who were already doing fine. Farmers and workers get a list, and the insiders get a summit.

fluid.zReason: Chips and EVs staying out is the right call, but China's list leaves out soybeans and the average only falls by about a point and a half, so the heartland hasn't gotten its buyer back.
fluid.text: Where are the soybeans? Farmers carried this trade fight, and China's list gives coal and timber a break but not the crop they need sold. Keeping chips and EVs off is right, but a point and a half off the average isn't a win for the heartland yet.

coalition.zReason: Getting Xi to Washington and keeping sensitive goods protected is real progress, but farm delivery depends on future rounds at APEC and the G20 that haven't happened yet.
coalition.text: I'll give Trump room: he got Xi here, kept the chips and EVs off the table, and there are more meetings coming. But I notice a lot of people I stand with ready to call anything he signs a win, and somebody has to ask where the soybeans are. Loyalty's fine. The farmers still need a buyer.

denominated.zReason: The speaker trusts Trump as the holder, so Xi coming to Washington counts as proof that pressure delivers, and the soybeans are expected to come later.
denominated.text: Trump made China come to him. The hawks kept their chips, and he's just getting started.

LF.text: A tariff cut is a price cut, and I'll take it. But going from 22% to 20.5% barely touches a tax households are still paying.

LC.text: I don't see much here for farm towns without soybeans, and I'd still ask the people on my side calling it a sellout to wait and see how it's implemented.

LD.text: It's a photo op. He built the wall and wants credit for putting in a door.

RF.text: Nonsensitive goods get normal rates, American timber and coal get into China, and the chips stay protected. That's the deal working as designed.

RC.text: It's a start. I'd tell the people I usually agree with to stop calling it a breakthrough while the soybeans are still missing.
keywords: the people I usually agree with

RD.text: Trump made China come to him. He's just getting started.

objectLayer.stated: Reciprocal tariff cuts on $30 billion of goods each way: a step toward normal trade after the Trump–Xi meeting.
objectLayer.operative: Most-favored-nation rates on nonsensitive goods (fireworks, tableware, timber, coal), with the strategic tariffs (chips, EVs, batteries) and soybeans untouched; the average U.S. tariff on Chinese goods moves about a point and a half, on terms and dates not yet published on the U.S. side.
objectLayer.inversion: Lean, not ruled: B fluid. The China-hawk institutional right, which built its case on tariffs as leverage over China, reads tariff cuts to China as the policy working; it keeps the sign by holding that the leverage (chips) survives. Partial, not a flip. A second lean at A coalition runs the other way: the free-trade left praising a Trump tariff cut, consistent with its own prior (tariffs as a consumer tax), so not an inversion.

blindAuthoring.authorNote: The hardest bands were D-coalition and C-coalition. On D's side, trust in Trump and the missing soybeans pull against each other, so the band sits close to zero, and that zero is honest ambivalence, not a hedge. C-coalition had to show the left-populist reflex without turning into a milder rim, and it does that by pointing to a real fact: the U.S. side's implementation details were not stated. The z I trust least is D-denominated at +0.55. R-0921-1 requires it to be positive because the speaker trusts Trump, but plenty of rim right-populists are farm-state voters, and the missing soybeans could pull them toward distrust. Its honest range is about +0.2 to +0.8, and a farm-anchored rim could sit near zero. A-denominated at -0.6 is the next most fragile; it could be anywhere from -0.3 to -0.7. The pattern: the centers are fairly tight, between about -0.45 and +0.45, and only the institutional right reads the lists as working as designed. The rim spread comes from trust in Trump, not from the goods. D is the one station whose rim goes positive while its fluid band is negative. The institutional left's fluid and coalition bands also split in sign, because its dislike of tariffs as a consumer tax works against its distrust of the person cutting them.

inversionLeans: B fluid (lean, not ruled): the China-hawk institutional right reads tariff cuts to China as the policy working; prior = the tariff-as-leverage case it has made since 2018 (coverage, not a live Reading). Partial: the band keeps its sign by holding that the chips leverage survives.
D fluid (lean): the right-populist center goes negative on a Trump trade deal over the missing soybeans, while its rim goes positive. A split inside the station, not a reversal of a prior.
